title: st.skeleton() - Implementation Proposal for space-filling empties.
body:
### Checklist

- [X] I have searched the [existing issues](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues) for similar feature requests.
- [X] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

I would like to work on adding a new container variation to Streamlit called `st.skeleton`. The `SkeletonElement` proto was added by [USER] in https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/pull/7598 as a way to allow the Streamlit Scriptrunner to display a small loading animation while it was still waiting to start rendering elements to the page. However, at the time, no means was added to allow Streamlit app developers to use the new Skeleton element themselves.

This proposal outlines how _I_ think the new `st.skeleton` feature should function. It is also a call for discussion -- if you think this feature goes too far or not far enough, please let me know. If you would personally find a feature like this useful, please upvote.

### Why?

I think the Skeleton element has significant value as a way to allow app developers to separate -- both structurally and temporally -- the definition of their app's UI from the sometimes-IO-constrained process of fetching and rendering data. **an `st.skeleton` as defined in this proposal thus represents the promise of content to the end application user**

### How?

`st.skeleton` is fundamentally just an `st.empty` with a future promise of additional content (typically just one chart or plot or table or "thing" per skeleton)

### Call Signature
```python
st.skeleton(width=0.5, height=100, callback=my_function, autocallback=False)
# Width and height of the skeleton are configurable. Fractional values for width are treated as a percentage, 
# while values >1 are treated as a minimum pixel size.
```

### What does it look like?
See https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/pull/7598
- May decide to add a third keywrod option to choose between an `AppSkeleton` and a `Skeleton` style animation but for now 

### What's the basic use case?
It's most basic use is a drop-in replacement for `st.empty()`. 
Like an empty, `st.skeleton()` returns a special SkeletonDeltaGenerator context manager object.
When you call another DeltaGenerator mixin function on it, it behaves just like an empty, and the skeleton animation that was playing is replaced by the new content. So this
```python
# Draw UI
st.write("Census Data")
census_data_placeholder = st.empty()  # The empty is a collapsed element
year = st.selectbox("Select Year", options=[2022, 2023, 2024])

# Get data from source
# assume function call takes a long time
census_dataframe = get_census_data_from_database(year)

# Draw the data, causing it to "pop" in above the year selectbox.
census_data_placeholder.dataframe(census_dataframe)
```
becomes
```python
# Draw UI
st.write("Census Data")
census_data_placeholder = st.skeleton(height=500px)  # The skeleton holds space for the future data
year = st.selectbox("Select Year", options=[2022, 2023, 2024])

# Get data from source, assume this takes a long time
census_dataframe = get_census_data_from_database(year)

# Draw the data, replacing the skeleton animation that was previously there
census_data_placeholder.dataframe(census_dataframe)
```

In this case (and as you will see below, in this case only) replacement can happen multiple times:
```python
skeleton = st.skeleton()

# User is shown a skeleton animation while data1 loads
data1 = get_data_long_running_function()
skeleton.dataframe(data1)

# User sees data1 while data2 loads, then data1 is replaced
data2 = get_data_another_long_running_function()
skeleton.dataframe(data2)
```

### Use as a context manager
When you use `st.skeleton()` in a `with` statement, it first places an `st.container` inside of itself
and then sets that as the DeltaGenerator context, allowing you to write natural code like:
```python
# Draw UI
st.write("Census Data")
census_data_placeholder = st.skeleton(height=500px)
year = st.selectbox("Select Year", options=[2022, 2023, 2024])

# Get data from source, assume this takes a long time
census_dataframe = get_census_data_from_database(year)
census_statistics = compute_statistics(census_dataframe)

# Draw the data, replacing the skeleton animation that was previously there
# Both the st.dataframe and the st.write are dispalyed inside of an st.container
# inside of the skeleton
with census_data_placeholder:
    st.dataframe(census_dataframe)
    st.write(census_statistics)
```

If only implemented up to this point in the proposal `st.skeleton` is still useful as a way to have an `st.empty` take up space in a page's UI. This avoids "pop-in" data that changes the layout of the UI significantly for the end user -- which is a problem that can currently happen with `st.empty`

### Getting fancy with callbacks
Going beyond basic `st.empty` functionality, `st.skeleton` also has a `callback` argument which allows you to queue up some function to be run at a later time. The callback function is assumed to itself call into one or more Streamlit elements. It can be run directly by calling `.load(*args, **kwargs)` on the `SkeletonDeltaGenerator`. The callback function acts as if it were being run inside a `with skeleton:` block, e.g.
```python
skeleton = st.skeleton(callback=my_function)
# ... more code
skeleton.load(a, b, c)
```
is equivalent to
```python
skeleton = st.skeleton()
# ... more code
with skeleton:
   my_function(a, b, c)
```

As an example:
```python
def render_census_data(year):
    # Get data from source, assume this takes a long time
    census_dataframe = get_census_data_from_database(year)
    census_statistics = compute_statistics(census_dataframe)
    # Draw the data
    st.dataframe(census_dataframe)
    st.write(census_statistics)

# Draw UI
st.write("Census Data")
census_data_placeholder = st.skeleton(height=500px, callback=render_census_data)
year = st.selectbox("Select Year", options=[2022, 2023, 2024])

# Load the census data and display it in place of the skeleton by running
# the callback function.
census_data_placeholder.load(year)
```

### Lions and Tigers and Autocallbacks, Oh my!
Where callbacks can _really_ shine is via an "autocallback" feature. This is a user-configurable feature which is enabled
by default. When an `st.skeleton()` call with a callback function is encountered, it will register itself with the current `ScriptRunner`. At the end of a successful and complete page execution, the ScriptRunner will then call `.load()` on all of the `SkeletonDeltaGenerator`s that meet the following criteria:
1. the `.load()` method was not already called on them by the user
2. they have a valid element path on the front end (meaning they haven't been _replaced_ by any other content yet)

`.load()` is called in the order that the `st.skeleton()` was first encountered. There may be additional limitations (such as enforcing that callback functions do not modify session_state or something like that.

When autocallback is enabled (by default), the st.skeleton() also accepts `args` and `kwargs` parameters since
there will be no calling of the `load` function.
```python
# Draw UI
st.write("Census Data")
year = st.selectbox("Select Year", options=[2022, 2023, 2024])
census_data_placeholder = st.skeleton(height=500px, callback=render_census_data, args=[year])

# The callback render_census_data is automatically called at the end of script execution with the argument `year`
```
Optional: the SkeletonDeltaGenerator also has a `.set_callback_arguments(*args, **kwargs)` method so that parameters
can be set even after the SkeletonDeltaGenerator is created
```python
# Draw UI
st.write("Census Data")
census_data_placeholder = st.skeleton(height=500px, callback=render_census_data)
year = st.selectbox("Select Year", options=[2022, 2023, 2024])
census_data_placeholder.set_callback_args(year)
```
And you can turn it off via a global config option or a keyword argument
```python
census_data_placeholder = st.skeleton(height=500px, callback=render_census_data, autocallback=False)
```

![Views](https://api.views-badge.org/badge/st-issue-8032)

[USER] Thanks for this detailed feature spec :) this is great 🎉 I personally think this would be a great addition: it's relatively simple to implement, it doesn't really add any significant tech debt and allows users to build a smoother app experience. However, new features will require internal discussions and decisions... and this is something that might take a bit of time :( 

The Streamlit-way is to minimize the number of parameters. So, if we get to an agreement on adding this to Streamlit, I'm pretty sure that we will want to ship - at least in the initial release - only with the `height` parameter. I think `height` has a significant benefit since we can lower some jumping effects since the developer can reserve space on the UI based on what he knows will render there. This isn't possible with anything else at the moment. The other parameters are a bit more nice-to-have, and could be something to add in a potential second iteration. 

one quick thought about `height`: If we just implement a configurable height for skeleton, it might not be enough to prevent the jumping effect since it might replace the user-defined skeleton with the automatic skeleton for a quick moment during the element loading. This is something we might want to prevent. 

btw. you can already use the app skeleton programmatically by using some internal logic:

```
from streamlit.proto.Skeleton_pb2 import Skeleton as SkeletonProto

st._main._enqueue("skeleton",  SkeletonProto())
```

Another potential way to add this functionality would be to only add a `height` parameter internally to SkeletonProto and then expose this functionality in [Streamlit extras](https://github.com/arnaudmiribel/streamlit-extras).

Thanks [USER]. Those are all good points. I'm happy to try to implement the basic element with a `height` parameter. I think it still has use for cases where the app takes a while to load data from an external source (but rendering that data is quick).

I might need some help from the Streamlit maintainers with the TSX side of things but we'll see how far it gets.

[USER] would someone on your teams have an opinion about adding this to Streamlit core lib vs. 

> add a height parameter internally to SkeletonProto and then expose this functionality in [Streamlit extras](https://github.com/arnaudmiribel/streamlit-extras).

As a minimum viable feature we could make this not even behave like an empty -- it just inserts a skeleton animation into the UI with a specified height. If you want it to be replaced by content, you just stick it in an empty by itself and then write over it. 

Users/streamlit extras could implement their own extensions on this, including all of the features mentioned in the original spec. And if it become widely used, perhaps those features could be brought into the core package.

```python
# Draw UI
st.write("Census Data")
census_data_placeholder = st.empty()
census_data_placeholder.skeleton(height=500px)  # The skeleton holds space for the future data
year = st.selectbox("Select Year", options=[2022, 2023, 2024])

# Get data from source, assume this takes a long time
census_dataframe = get_census_data_from_database(year)

# Draw the data, replacing the skeleton animation that was previously there
with census_data_placeholder.container():
   st.dataframe(census_dataframe)
   st.write(f"Data for {year} loaded successfully")
```

[USER] The skeleton implementation already has the `empty` behavior, so this is "for free" :)

```
from streamlit.proto.Skeleton_pb2 import Skeleton as SkeletonProto

skeleton_proto = SkeletonProto()
skeleton_placeholder = st._main._enqueue("skeleton", skeleton_proto)

# Some code

skeleton_placeholder.dataframe(...)
```

Just came across this old issue, random thought I had: maybe `st.skeleton` would actually be more intuitive if we do it similarly to `st.spinner`:

```python
with st.skeleton(width="stretch", height=300):
    data = load_data()
st.dataframe(data, height=300)
```

So the `with` here is not a container (which feels a bit weird to me in the proposal above, where we basically have a container, but it's filled with an element to begin with), but just a simple timing thing that's similar to `st.spinner` – once the content is loaded, the skeleton goes away (and in the case above is replaced by a dataframe of the same size). 

The example from the original issue above (where the skeleton/dataframe are displayed above a selectbox) could then be handled with the normal `st.empty` pattern:

```
st.write("Census Data")
census_data_placeholder = st.empty()
year = st.selectbox("Select Year", options=[2022, 2023, 2024])

with census_data_placeholder.skeleton():
    census_dataframe = get_census_data_from_database(year)
    census_statistics = compute_statistics(census_dataframe)

with census_data_placeholder.container():
    st.dataframe(census_dataframe)
    st.write(census_statistics)
```

## Update

An `st.skeleton` element will be released in 1.59 which can be used in two usage modes:

1. **Standalone mode** (like `st.empty()`): Returns a replaceable placeholder
   ```python
   placeholder = st.skeleton(height=200)
   # ... load data ...
   placeholder.dataframe(df)  # Replaces skeleton with content
   ```

2. **Context manager mode** (like `st.spinner()`): Shown after a short delay while the block runs and auto-clears on exit
   ```python
   with st.skeleton(height=100):
       # ... loading happens here ...
   # Skeleton automatically clears when block exits
   ```

**Parameters:**
- `height`: int, `"stretch"`, or `None` (default: `None`). `None` uses the standard element height (same as most input widgets); an integer sets a fixed pixel height; `"stretch"` fills a parent container with a bounded height.
- `width`: int or `"stretch"` (default: `"stretch"`)
